franklin-search-042.description: The moment Henry Kellett's people left the Resolute and Intrepid, at seven in the evening of 15 May 1854, as George Frederick M'Dougall, the Resolute's master, described it: 'After advancing about a quarter of a mile, the crews of the various sledges halted simultaneously; unharnessed, and gave three hearty cheers for the Resolute and Intrepid; but though the ice is a good conductor of sound, we heard no response.' Francis Leopold McClintock, who had walked Sir Edward Belcher's orders in from Beechey Island a fortnight before, commanded the Intrepid. Forty-two men then dragged four sledges east across Barrow Strait for thirteen days to reach the North Star at Beechey Island; sledge loads averaged 215 lb a man.

franklin-search-062.description: The best contemporary count of the meat tins on Beechey Island, made by the party under Alexander Stewart, master of the brig Sophia, that William Penny sent across on 27 August 1850: 'The meat-tins were piled up in heaps in the same regular manner as shot is piled up... Six or seven hundred tins were counted, and many more besides these were dug up and emptied out in search of documents.' Every one of them was opened by the searchers of 1850 in the hope that a record had been buried in it.

franklin-search-074.description: The arithmetic of an overland wintering, set out by John Richardson at Fort Confidence in September 1848, with John Rae as his second: 'We had in all forty-two souls to provide for, exclusive of Indians coming casually on our store.' The next day eighteen of them - three Canadians to the Big Island fishery and eleven English sappers and seamen who could be spared - were sent away, and 'being thus relieved from the maintenance of eighteen people, the resources of the post were considered equal to feeding the remainder, and I looked forward to the winter without anxiety.' Naval expeditions carried their food with them; overland ones lived on the country and counted mouths.

franklin-search-078.description: The depot that Commander William John Samuel Pullen's people from HMS North Star built on the beach at Beechey Island while the ship lay there through the winters of 1852-53 and 1853-54, using spars and timber including some from the wrecked Breadalbane. It was stocked as a refuge in case Franklin's men, or any of Sir Edward Belcher's, came out that way, and it was still being drawn on by later expeditions; Francis Leopold McClintock called there in the Fox in August 1858. What stands there now is a ruin - collapsed walls and scattered barrel staves - alongside the four graves and the monument that carries the memorial tablets to Franklin's men, to Belcher's dead and to Joseph Rene Bellot. The whole site is a National Historic Site and is protected; visitors go ashore only under the conditions agreed with Parks Canada and the community of Qausuittuq (Resolute).

franklin-search-113.description: A sledge party crossing broken ice, engraved for Francis Leopold McClintock's narrative. It stands for the spring journeys of 1859 out of Port Kennedy - McClintock down the east side of King William Island, William Hobson down the west, Allen Young over Prince of Wales Island - which found the Victory Point record, the boat on its sledge in Erebus Bay, and the skeletons.

franklin-search-115.description: The large folding map at the end of Francis Leopold McClintock's narrative, laying out the archipelago as it stood after the Fox's voyage, with the search tracks and the ground covered on King William Island where Franklin's people died. It is the first published chart to show the whole circuit of King William Island, completed by McClintock and Hobson in 1859.
